#5182. “I’ll Block for This”: Ripple’s Schwartz Sets Reply Rules

Home » Ripple (XRP) » “I’ll Block for This”: Ripple’s Schwartz Sets Reply Rules

The move follows a rise in negative XRP commentary that has little to do with the actual threads.

David Schwartz, known on X as JoelKatz and one of the original architects of the XRP Ledger, has begun blocking accounts that insert crypto-related comments or accusations into his non-crypto conversations.

Schwartz explained that a growing number of people are responding to his replies on unrelated topics with crypto content or insults. When that happens, the people he is talking to end up with their followers seeing the off-topic posts.

He described the pattern as forcing those users into a choice: either tolerate the spam or block him. To avoid that outcome, he has started blocking the accounts responsible.

A significant share of the posts, he noted, accuse him of fraud or scamming. He stated he will block this behavior regardless of whether the comment is framed as XRP criticism or praise.

Schwartz drew a distinction between relevant criticism and irrelevant spam. He wrote that he does not mind people criticizing him or accusing him of wrongdoing, provided the posts contain actual content and avoid simple slurs.

Recently, there's been a significant increase in people responding to replies of mine that have nothing to do with crypto with insults or crypto content. I hate to do it, but I pretty much have to block for this because otherwise the people I'm replying to have no choice but to…

The condition is placement: such comments should appear in the critic’s own threads or in replies to his posts where the topic has at least some relevance.

What he said he will not tolerate is users following him across X specifically to insert “scammer” or even positive XRP comments into conversations that have nothing to do with crypto. Those replies, he argued, anger the people whose threads are being used.

For anyone already blocked under this policy, Schwartz left an opening. He said that if the person promises not to repeat the behavior and finds a way to get his attention, he will unblock them.

The offer stands even if the user continues to strongly dislike him. The stated limit is simple: do not use his replies to spam other people’s followers.

Some replies eagerly pushed back, arguing that frustration with Ripple’s performance or past expectations justified the critical comments. Others framed the blocks as an attempt to avoid accountability.

Can I honestly say that I have nothing to do with the price of XRP? I guess probably not nothing. But very little. pic.twitter.com/8Plpyw61IZ

Schwartz’s post itself focused on the practical problem of irrelevant replies landing in other users’ timelines rather than on any broader debate about XRP or Ripple.

The new policy amounts to a clear boundary on where and how he is willing to engage on the platform. Criticism remains acceptable in relevant spaces. Off-topic insertions into unrelated conversations, whether hostile or not, are now grounds for a block.

#5180. Zcash Upgrade Could Lock $16 Million in Crypto Forever

Zcash Upgrade Could Lock $16 Million in Crypto Forever

At recent market prices, those holdings represent roughly $15 million to $16 million that could become effectively frozen when the network activates its NU7 upgrade.

“NU7 (block 3,543,405) makes v4 transactions invalid, so what remains in Sprout is unspendable: frozen, not burned,” Zecstats says in its information card for Sprout.

The upgrade is scheduled for block 3,543,405, expected Thursday evening in the United States. The exact deadline depends on how quickly the blockchain processes new blocks, rather than a predetermined clock time.

Unlike Bitcoin, where transactions are generally visible to anyone examining the blockchain, Zcash allows users to conceal transaction amounts and the addresses involved. It accomplishes this through technology called zero-knowledge proofs, which can verify that a transaction is valid without revealing its private details.

NU7 changes that by eliminating version-4 transactions, the only format capable of moving coins out of Sprout. According to the network's technical specification, transactions using that format will become invalid after activation.

The decision addresses a problem familiar to anyone maintaining old software: supporting obsolete technology creates additional complexity and potential security vulnerabilities.

Developers haven't technically destroyed the coins. They will continue counting toward Zcash's circulating issuance calculations, and a future network upgrade could theoretically restore access, but that is not guaranteed, and the team has not shown any interest in doing so.

In fact, the specification explicitly warns that spending those funds may never be re-enabled.

Legacy holders are the people most exposed to the change. Anyone whose ZEC remains in Sprout must move it through a compatible withdrawal mechanism before the upgrade activates, or risk losing access indefinitely.

Sprout addresses begin with "zc," which can help users recognize old wallet records. Regular ZEC holders using modern supported wallets do not need to migrate their coins out of Sprout, although keeping wallet software updated remains important.

The blockchain also cannot reveal who owns the remaining Sprout balance, meaning nobody knows how much belongs to active users and how much is already inaccessible because its owners lost their keys.

Meanwhile, NU7 brings a benefit for everyone else: Zcash's target block interval falls from 75 seconds to 25 seconds, meaning transactions should receive their first confirmation approximately three times faster, according to the Zcash Foundation.

For Sprout holders, however, the relevant number is block 3,543,405 which will happen later today. As of the time of publication, the latest available block is 3,543,027. Once the network reaches block 3,543,405, any remaining coins in the old pool will be frozen under the new rules.

#5178. US drops a proposed crypto rule. Europe can still hold up your $500 transfer

The US has withdrawn its proposed $250 transfer threshold, but missing identity information can still hold up even a $500 payment at an EU exchange.

FinCEN, the U.S. financial-crime regulator, and the Federal Reserve announced Nov. 6 that they are withdrawing a plan to expand transfer-data duties to cross-border payments as small as $250. Existing U.S. requirements remain, alongside EU information checks that can affect even a $500 crypto payment.

An illustrative $500 customer transfer from a U.S. exchange to an EU exchange shows the limit of the retreat. It is below the U.S. Travel Rule's $3,000 threshold, but the receiving exchange's EU obligations can still prevent the recipient from accessing the assets until required information is supplied.

The joint withdrawal notice was published in the Federal Register on Nov. 9, with withdrawal effective that day. FinCEN's Nov. 6 announcement confirmed the decision. The proposed $250 threshold never took effect through this rulemaking.

The October 2020 proposal would have lowered the threshold for specified recordkeeping and information-transmission duties from $3,000 to $250 for transfers beginning or ending outside the United States.

The existing Recordkeeping Rule requires covered institutions to collect and retain transfer information, while the Travel Rule requires information to pass to other institutions in the payment chain. The joint notice describes the current threshold as $3,000 or more. Withdrawing the proposal avoids extending those duties into the lower-value band.

The agencies cite the passage of more than five years, the value of further public feedback and changes in virtual-currency markets and legal frameworks. They say any future similar amendments should reflect those developments.

Existing crypto compliance duties continue. FinCEN's 2019 virtual-currency guidance says qualifying convertible-virtual-currency transfers of $3,000 or more can trigger Travel Rule requirements. Covered money transmitters also retain applicable anti-money-laundering programs, customer-identification controls, recordkeeping, monitoring and reporting obligations.

The EU's crypto-transfer regulation, applicable since Dec. 30, 2024, covers customer transfers involving a crypto-asset service provider with its registered office in the EU. Its information requirements have no general exemption for small crypto transfers. The regulation explains that crypto transfers should face the same requirements regardless of amount or whether they are domestic or cross-border.

For the hypothetical $500 payment, assume the receiving exchange is an EU-registered provider serving a customer. The relevant duties here belong to the EU receiving provider; the U.S. exchange's own obligations are governed separately.

Qualitative illustration from the joint notice, FinCEN CVC guidance and EU Articles 2,14-17. $500 is hypothetical, not an observed payment. Arrows show responsibilities and information flow, not speed, volume or legal reach over a US-only sender.

Scope: ordinary customer exchange-to-exchange crypto transfer with an EU-registered receiving provider. Other controls may apply. The separate self-hosted-address test and provider-free P2P exemption are outside this diagram. No processing-time or failure estimate.

Article 14 specifies sender and recipient names, relevant blockchain addresses and applicable crypto-account identifiers. Sender information also includes an address and country, official document number and customer identification number, or alternatively a date and place of birth. Additional legal-entity identifiers are conditional.

Providers can exchange that information in secure messages separate from the blockchain transaction. The EU receiving provider must detect missing information and verify recipient information before making the assets available; qualifying previous identity verification can satisfy the latter check.

If required details are missing or incomplete, Article 17 requires the receiving provider to act on a risk-sensitive basis and without undue delay. It must reject or return the transfer, or request the required information before making the assets available. Its procedures can include suspension.

That is how blockchain arrival and access to funds can diverge: the assets can arrive while the exchange still needs information before releasing them to its customer.

The regulation adds an ownership-or-control assessment for transfers exceeding €1,000 to or from self-hosted addresses. Smaller transfers still face the applicable information requirements. The exchange-to-exchange example falls under those general rules rather than this self-hosted-address test.

Scope matters, too. Person-to-person crypto transfers without a service provider fall outside the regulation, as do transfers where both providers act on their own behalf. An ordinary customer payment between exchanges remains within the provider-based framework.

The European Banking Authority's applicable guidelines address detecting missing information and managing transfers that lack it.

#5177. North Korean Hackers Flip Stolen Binance Funds Into NEAR Meme Coins

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

North Korea's TraderTraitor group has started laundering funds stolen from Binance through newly created meme tokens, according to Elliptic.

The $6.4 billion Binance hack took place in October 2026 and was attributed to TraderTraitor.

According to Elliptic, the hackers have used this technique on Tron and NEAR, while a similar approach has appeared on Solana.

Between Nov. 5 and 7, 2026, the hackers launched at least six of these tokens on NEAR: FUK, OLCCL, MEILI, MMLI, DABI and SINU. Launching one cost around 25 NEAR (about $90).

According to Elliptic, the hackers paired each token with NEAR in a liquidity pool on a decentralized exchange (DEX). Wallets holding stolen NEAR deposited it into the pool and received the new token. A second set of wallets then sold the token back into the pool and withdrew NEAR.

This way, the funds never move directly from the wallets holding stolen assets to the receiving wallets.

According to Elliptic, the receiving wallets look like ordinary traders who sold a token at a profit.

Each token got typical meme branding, from monkeys to an image of Elon Musk under an "Elon 2028 President" banner. Elliptic noted that Musk is not linked to the tokens.

Each token was sold for the first time less than three hours after launch, and at least 75% of its trading took place within one day. None of the six tokens has traded since Nov. 8, and the creators of four of them withdrew the remaining liquidity on that day.

In total, 117,000 NEAR (about $421,000) moved through the scheme. Most of it then went into stablecoins or to a cross-chain bridge.

Elliptic noted that five of the six token creators received funds from a wallet that had been selling the previous token 2 to 13 minutes before the new launch, and in this way the operation funded itself.

The only outside activity was a few small purchases of FUK on its first day, which accounted for less than 1% of its volume, Elliptic said.

According to Elliptic, the on-chain trail stays public, and the technique makes tracing the funds slower. The hackers can also create many tokens and abandon each one after use.

In 2025, after the Bybit hack, the same scheme moved at least $24 million through Tron. In that case, the hackers paired a worthless token with a stablecoin.

In the Binance case, Elliptic identified a similar token on Tron on Nov. 2. On Nov. 3, stolen SOL was swapped into existing thinly traded tokens on Solana and then sold for USDC.

Elliptic said that so far only a small part of the stolen funds has gone through meme tokens. About 11.8 million NEAR from the theft has not moved yet, and at press time, NEAR is trading at $3.60, which puts these funds at around $42.4 million.

Elliptic also advises compliance teams to check funds coming from liquidity pools, especially pools with newly created tokens.

"Laundering is a race to move funds before they are flagged," Elliptic added.

#5175. Bitcoin Lightning’s security update shuts one door. A critical Linux flaw remains

LND’s October 30 update blocks a demonstrated attack route, but affected, unpatched Linux hosts still need a kernel fix and reboot.

Bitcoin Lightning operators running an affected, unpatched Linux kernel remain exposed to a critical vulnerability after upgrading LND, the software used to operate their payment nodes.

Its October 30 releases, v0.20.7-beta and v0.21.6-beta, disable Multipath TCP, or MPTCP, listeners by default. That closes the demonstrated CVE-2026-98432 route through those listeners. It leaves the kernel flaw in place and does not cover other services on the same machine.

Another exposed MPTCP service on the same unpatched machine can preserve the demonstrated route, even after LND’s default listeners have changed.

The flaw involves freed memory being used during IPv4 TCP connection handling in Linux and can allow an attacker to run code on an affected host. Ubuntu assigns it a critical CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8.

LND’s operator notes say Go 1.24 and later enabled MPTCP listeners by default on Linux, which LND 0.21.x consequently exposed on its peer, gRPC and REST ports. These include the node’s connections to other nodes and its application interfaces.

The Go Security Team’s advisory explains why that change cannot finish the job. The demonstrated exploit requires an exposed MPTCP listener, but the kernel bug is broader. Similar attacks against systems without MPTCP listeners may be possible; the advisory does not establish a demonstrated non-MPTCP exploit.

Go also warns that disabling MPTCP one program at a time is fragile. A single remaining exposed listener leaves the system vulnerable to that route, and explicit socket settings can override Go’s default configuration.

The advisories describe a demonstrated Linux exploit, not evidence that attackers used this flaw against LND nodes or stole Bitcoin.

CryptoSlate previously covered the same CVE’s implications for Solana validators. The Core Lightning channel and remote-command fixes reported November 6 concern separate application flaws.

The Ubuntu tracker, checked November 9 and last updated November 7, still labeled the standard linux package for Ubuntu 24.04 LTS vulnerable, with work in progress in 6.8.0-149.149. Its Ubuntu 22.04 LTS entry carried the same status for 5.15.0-203.213.

Patch availability varies by package. In its November 2 advisory, Canonical said kernel fixes for this CVE were available in the -proposed repository for users who run their own kernel acceptance tests, while qualification testing continued.

Ubuntu’s work-in-progress newsletter for November 1–7 also said some releases, including 24.04, had advanced to -updates. That broader note does not identify every kernel variant. Operators therefore need to check the available update for their exact kernel package rather than infer availability from the Ubuntu release name alone.

The tracker illustrates the distinction: it lists the standard Ubuntu 26.10 linux package as fixed in 7.3.0-10.10, while cloud, hardware-enablement and other kernel variants have separate entries. A fixed status for one package cannot settle the status of another.

LND maintainers recommend upgrading the application, disabling MPTCP on the host, and installing a patched kernel as soon as the distribution makes one available.

Illustrative configuration: LND’s default MPTCP listeners are off, but another service still exposes one on an unpatched host.

With MPTCP disabled across relevant network namespaces, the demonstrated route is closed. The underlying kernel flaw remains.

After a patched kernel is installed and booted, this kernel flaw is repaired. The diagram retains the preceding MPTCP mitigation.

Illustrative configurations, not tests of a live node or a record of attacks. Disabling MPTCP covers the demonstrated route only; the bug is broader. The disabled state assumes relevant network namespaces are covered. Other vulnerabilities are outside scope.

Their guidance uses sudo sysctl -w net.mptcp.enabled=0 for the host setting, with a persistent configuration to retain it. The setting applies per network namespace, so Docker deployments need separate attention to the container’s network configuration. Changing the host alone is not a substitute for checking that scope.

Operators who cannot upgrade LND immediately can start their existing binary with GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0 to disable Go’s default MPTCP listeners. Maintainers warn against re-enabling that default before patching the kernel.

Canonical advises checking the kernel actually running with uname -r. After installing its kernel security update, a reboot is required. An upgraded LND binary and an installed kernel package are different milestones; completing the operating-system repair requires running the patched kernel.

#5174. Shiba Inu (SHIB) Holder Count Surges Amid Severe Price Correction

The leading meme-based crypto asset, Shiba Inu, has continued to face a severe price drop amid prolonged crypto market volatility, yet its user activity has remained positive.

While uncertainty caused by its frequent price fluctuations has persisted, it appears that new users have remained enthusiastic about the leading meme token project, and they have continued to join the Shiba Inu ecosystem.

Latest on-chain data from Etherscan shows that the Shiba Inu holder count has now reached 1,698,454 as of today, November 9, following the consistent growth seen in the past day.

This means that a total of 2,025 new SHIB holders have been added to the ecosystem since the new month began, signaling sustained user growth even while its price performance has been extremely weak so far in November.

While the consistent increase in SHIB holders has been accompanied by a persistent decline in its price and slowed on-chain activity, it remains uncertain whether the rise in the number of holders could be pointed to increasing accumulation.

The surge in SHIB holders has drawn attention from market analysts as it comes after the network witnessed slow adoption late last month as nearly 2,500 wallet addresses holding the meme coin disappeared within just two days.

Nonetheless, it appears that interest in the meme token is picking pace again as a decent number of users continue to join in everyday, positioning it to hit the long-anticipated 1,700,000 holder milestone this month as Shiba Inu currently needs to add only 1,546 more holders to hit this key level.

#5172. Charles Schwab Expands Crypto Trading to SOL, AVAX and LINK, XRP Not Included

American brokerage giant Charles Schwab has announced that it is expanding its crypto trading platform, Schwab Crypto, with the addition of Solana (SOL), Avalanche (AVAX) and Chainlink (LINK) for trading.

The three new coins expand the existing list of two cryptocurrencies, Bitcoin (BTC) and Ethereum (ETH), that can be traded directly. This now means that users can trade five cryptocurrencies directly on the platform.

Notably, however, XRP, one of the largest cryptocurrencies by market cap, is still missing from the list of available coins.

In its official press release, Schwab's head of digital assets, Joe Vietri, underlined the brokerage's commitment to further expanding its crypto trading options.

Also, the company confirmed that it will be adding more cryptocurrencies and digital assets going forward. But it didn't specify whether this includes XRP.

Although XRP is not offered directly on the Schwab Crypto trading platform, it is still available to Schwab users in one way or another.

Charles Schwab offers standard and micro futures contracts on XRP through its thinkorswim platform.

In July 2025, the company pointed out the availability of XRP futures with the ticker /XRP and also smaller micro contracts with the ticker /MXP.

It further expanded its derivatives trading platform with the addition of almost 24/7 trading for certain crypto futures, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and XRP, in June 2026.

Charles Schwab's aggressive approach to the crypto industry has been noticeable throughout 2026.

First, the company officially announced Schwab Crypto on April 16. In this announcement, it outlined its plans to introduce direct trading of Bitcoin and Ethereum for retail users.

The next major development came on Oct. 15, when Rick Wurster, the CEO of Charles Schwab, confirmed the introduction of crypto transfers.

The platform now allows eligible customers to transfer eligible crypto assets to and from external wallets through the Schwab Crypto platform. However, this is not yet available to all customers. Access is being rolled out gradually.

In August 2026, the exact shift in volume arrived on the same day as XRP’s price rebound, which is why Bitrue Research Institute’s study recommends watching these signals together.

The outlined three-month setup works like a swiss clock: with the 14-day RSI below chasing down levels below 35, that’s usually bullish for XRP. #5170. Two Bitcoin miners reported nearly $2 billion in profit. The biggest boost wasn’t cash

Core Scientific and TeraWulf’s reported profits include large non-cash gains. Their operating results and construction cash flows tell different stories.

Core Scientific and TeraWulf reported nearly $1.9 billion of combined third-quarter profit as they shifted from Bitcoin mining toward data-center hosting for AI customers. Their earnings included $1.76 billion of pretax non-cash gains from revaluing financial instruments.

The November 5 Core Scientific disclosure and November 6 TeraWulf disclosure show different operating outcomes for the quarter ended September 30, 2026. Core earned $72 million in operating income under U.S. accounting rules; TeraWulf recorded an $88 million operating loss. Core's operating result itself included a $19 million digital-asset fair-value gain. Hosting now supplies most of both companies' revenue, following their shift from Bitcoin mining toward computing leases. Assessing whether the conversions fund themselves requires the separate cash-flow and financing disclosures.

Core’s $1,178 million consolidated net income and TeraWulf’s $710 million add up to approximately $1.89 billion.

In Core's filing, the $1,034 million revaluation gain comprised $964 million on legacy Tranche 1 and Tranche 2 warrants, $69 million on the liability portion of an AMD warrant and $1 million on contingent value rights. Legacy instruments supplied the largest component of Core's gain.

Warrants give holders rights to buy shares. Core's AMD warrant accompanied July customer leases, with its issuance value recorded as an incentive reducing future lease revenue. Its liability portion is remeasured through earnings. Core attributed changes in its broader warrant and contingent-value line primarily to stock-price changes.

TeraWulf's $728 million gain came from revaluing Google warrants issued in exchange for credit support covering certain Fluidstack lease obligations. The credit support can help finance projects. Remeasurement raises reported earnings through a non-cash accounting entry.

The revaluation gains enter earnings before tax, while the net-income figures also reflect tax effects and other gains. Core also recorded a $106.5 million tax benefit, primarily from releasing part of a valuation allowance associated with its Polaris acquisition. TeraWulf recorded a $95 million gain on selling its Abernathy joint-venture stake.

Core Scientific and TeraWulf reported $1.89bn in consolidated Q3 net income alongside $1.76bn of pretax non-cash revaluation gains.

Legacy warrants supplied most of Core's $1.034bn pretax revaluation gain. Its AMD warrant is a separate lease-linked instrument.

Google warrants supporting Fluidstack leases produced TeraWulf's $728.4m non-cash gain. Credit support and cash proceeds are distinct.

Large accounting gains can lift net income while operating results diverge.

Net income is after tax; revaluation gains are before tax. Separate scales compare earnings and operating results. These measures differ from cash flow and cannot establish construction-funding adequacy.

Q3 ended September 30, 2026. USD millions. Reported figures rounded from filings. Net-income bars share a 0 to $1,200m scale; operating bars use a separate symmetric ±$100m scale. Core instrument gains sum to $1,034.358m before rounding. No pretax gain is subtracted from after-tax income.

Net income is after tax; revaluation gains are before tax. Separate scales compare earnings and operating results. These measures differ from cash flow and cannot establish construction-funding adequacy.

The difference also reaches per-share results: Core reported $3.42 basic earnings versus $0.47 diluted, while TeraWulf reported $1.42 basic earnings and a $0.03 diluted loss. The diluted calculations include warrant-gain reversals in the earnings used per share, alongside share-count adjustments.

Hosting growth is visible in both companies' sales. Core's colocation revenue reached $215 million out of $233 million in total sales, up from $137 million in the preceding quarter. Colocation gross profit was $128 million at a reported 60% margin.

TeraWulf generated $63 million of high-performance computing (HPC) lease revenue, approximately 83% of its $76 million total. Its $11 million HPC segment profit excludes expenses including corporate overhead and depreciation that enter consolidated operating results, giving it a different expense allocation from Core's colocation gross profit.

For the nine months ended September 30, Core generated $296 million of operating cash while spending $1,495 million on property, plant and equipment and another $677 million on asset acquisitions. Net financing cash inflow was $3,200 million.

Over that same nine-month period, TeraWulf used $179 million of operating cash and spent $2,231 million on plant and equipment purchases and deposits. It received $1,010 million of net financing cash, including approximately $1,200 million from common-stock issuance.

Core says conversions for hosting customer CoreWeave are largely funded by that customer. Development under its AMD and other cloud-customer arrangements will require additional external financing. It plans project-level bond financing. Management says existing liquidity plus anticipated funding sources support planned development and operating needs.

TeraWulf's Abernathy sale supplied $250 million of cash during Q3, distinct from the accounting gain; further installments remained expected. After quarter-end, it increased revolving-credit commitments to about $400 million, with an additional conditional, uncommitted $150 million expansion option. Its post-quarter November 4 Google credit support for leases with customer Anthropic concerns anticipated project financing. The Fluidstack warrants behind Q3's gain relate to a separate arrangement.

For the next phase, the operating split provides a more useful starting point than the combined profit: Core has reached positive operating income, while TeraWulf still reports an operating loss. Delivered hosting capacity, cash collections and financing commitments will determine how much of the construction bill the growing businesses can carry.

#5167. Ripple's Schwartz Debunks XRP Price Myth

David Schwartz, the former chief technology officer at Ripple and one of the creators of the XRP Ledger (XRPL), has dispelled one of the most common myths regarding the key factors that could impact the price of XRP.

The former Ripple CTO took to the X social media platform to challenge the idea that the use of XRP as the native gas token of the XRP Ledger could be a major factor in determining the price of the cryptocurrency.

"I don't think anybody who knows anything has said that the use of XRP as gas will be a major driver of the price of XRP," Schwartz wrote.

The comment was made as the Ripple veteran took part in the ever-growing debate centered around the poor price performance of XRP and the place of the cryptocurrency in Ripple's ever-expanding ecosystem.

The former Ripple CTO directed the audience's attention to a post from November 2025, in which he explained his thoughts on how mass adoption of the XRP Ledger could lead to greater value for the ledger's native cryptocurrency.

"The increased use and adoption of XRPL will add value to XRP by its privileged place on the ledger," Schwartz said.

He emphasized that XRP has several unique properties, including the lack of counterparty risk, the fact that it's jurisdictionless, and its privileged place in the network's autobridging features.

In addition, Schwartz argued that it would be hard to imagine the XRP Ledger succeeding on a mass scale without XRP capturing a significant portion of the value created by such success.

"I really do think it's hard to think we could end up in a world where XRPL is successful and XRP doesn't get a good fraction of that value," he said.

Nevertheless, Schwartz also said earlier that the XRP Ledger was not created with the sole intent of pushing the price of XRP higher. Instead, the original goal was to create a fast and cheap payment system with a native digital asset and a decentralized exchange feature.

Schwartz's recent comments come as frustration among XRP holders over the poor performance of the cryptocurrency is on the rise.

As of Monday, the Ripple-related token was trading at around the $1.09 level, down more than 12% in the last seven days.

Recently, Schwartz admitted that his influence on the market price of XRP is very small.

"Do I have anything to do with the price of XRP? Honestly? I guess probably not anything. But very little," he wrote during another interaction with critics.

#5166. The missing step in the warning that Japan could trigger Bitcoin’s next selloff

Japan’s overseas profits can stay overseas. A Bitcoin selloff needs more than an accounting surplus: watch actual money flows and leveraged positions.

Japan’s overseas profits can keep growing without the cash returning home. Bank of Japan Gov. Kazuo Ueda’s newly published International Monetary Fund lecture explains that distinction, complicating the case for treating Japan’s income surplus as an automatic source of yen buying and selling pressure on Bitcoin.

Ueda delivered the lecture on November 6, 2026, and the BOJ published it November 7. He described how substantial earnings from overseas affiliates stay invested abroad, sustaining Japan’s external income while adding to foreign direct investment.

CryptoSlate’s earlier coverage of Japanese foreign-debt selling examined how a shift toward domestic bonds could affect Bitcoin’s financing backdrop. The new lecture explains why overseas income alone cannot establish that shift.

For Bitcoin, the implications depend on what investors actually do with their money. A gradual shift toward Japanese assets could affect financing conditions; a leveraged yen carry unwind could generate much faster selling across markets. Neither can be read directly from an income-surplus headline.

In the lecture, Ueda said outward foreign direct investment has overtaken portfolio investment as Japan’s dominant capital-outflow vehicle since 2012. Direct investment concerns ownership in overseas businesses; portfolio investment concerns securities holdings.

Retained affiliate profits help explain the difference. Earnings generated abroad contribute to Japan’s primary income surplus, while reinvesting those earnings abroad is recorded as fresh direct investment. The same accounting process can therefore enlarge both income and outward investment without requiring that cash first return to Japan.

Ueda’s November 2026 lecture explains the retained-profit loop. Two separate financial channels show how Bitcoin could become exposed.

Conditional analysis: sustained preference for domestic assets could change financing conditions. Securities flows do not establish yen conversion or Bitcoin sales.

Historical mechanism: BIS researchers said leverage and margin pressure appeared to amplify August 2024 turbulence. Crypto losses suggested possible forced position closures.

Recorded income is distinct from yen buying. Portfolio shifts and leveraged unwinds require different evidence.

The diagrams do not measure current repatriation, currency conversion, carry positions or Bitcoin sales. The leverage loop describes an August 2024 mechanism, not a November 2026 unwind.

Qualitative, source-bound flow diagrams. The retained-profit loop follows Ueda; the selectable routes distinguish conditional portfolio reallocation from the BIS's historical leverage mechanism. Arrows show relationships, not flow amounts or measured speed.

The diagrams do not measure current repatriation, currency conversion, carry positions or Bitcoin sales. The leverage loop describes an August 2024 mechanism, not a November 2026 unwind.

Ueda also described more active domestic investment. Yet he said Japan’s foreign-asset stock and the continuing return advantage of overseas investments would keep primary income an enduring part of its external accounts. That combination allows stronger investment at home alongside continued earnings abroad.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

The latest available weekly evidence runs against a simple foreign-asset liquidation story. Japan’s Ministry of Finance (MOF) reported on November 6 that the designated Japanese reporting institutions were net buyers of foreign long-term debt and foreign equity and investment-fund shares during October 25–31.

The next checks are close. The ministry’s release schedule lists October’s monthly securities transactions for November 10 and weekly transactions covering November 1–7 for November 12, both at 8:50 a.m. Japan time. The schedule is subject to change; as of November 9, those results are still ahead.

These releases can help show whether reported foreign-security purchases or disposals persist. Their scope matters: MOF’s methodology covers designated major institutions, excludes direct investment and reserve assets, and does not capture every portfolio transaction. It also includes bond redemptions in disposals and provides no quotation-currency breakdown.

A run of net disposals would consequently be evidence about securities allocation. Establishing that the proceeds were converted into yen would require more information.

A yen carry trade is a financing position. Investors borrow a lower-yielding currency to invest in higher-yielding assets denominated in other currencies, sometimes using derivatives. That differs from a Japanese company retaining an overseas subsidiary’s profits.

In an August 2024 analysis, researchers at the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) described how deleveraging and increased margin requirements appeared to amplify market turbulence, with yen-funded carry positions particularly exposed. A stronger yen can make an unhedged yen borrowing position more costly to repay, while higher margins can force investors to find cash or cut exposure.

The researchers said that episode’s crypto losses suggested retail margin calls and possible forced closures of otherwise unrelated positions. Those historical findings illustrate a possible transmission channel, rather than establishing forced Bitcoin selling now.

The distinction changes what would strengthen the risk case. Persistent foreign-security disposals would support an allocation shift. Sharper yen moves accompanied by funding and margin stress would be more relevant to a leveraged unwind. Continued outward investment and retained earnings would weaken the claim that overseas profits must immediately drain into yen.

#5165. Online Gaming, Crypto Payments and On-Chain Games Are Different Categories

Home » Uncategorized » Online Gaming, Crypto Payments and On-Chain Games Are Different Categories

Online gaming, crypto payments, and blockchain gaming are not the same thing. Learn how to distinguish payment methods, game mechanics, and on-chain execution when evaluating crypto-enabled gaming platforms.

A wallet button beside a game does not explain where its rules run. A token ticker does not reveal who maintains the game state. Even a transaction recorded on a blockchain may describe a payment rather than a move inside the game. For readers assessing gaming products, these details matter because three separate ideas are often compressed into one label: access through the internet, payment with cryptocurrency, and execution on a blockchain.

An online game uses a network connection for some part of its operation. That could involve downloading content, joining a match, checking an account, or sending actions to a server. The browser or installed app supplies the interface, while processing can be divided between the player’s device and remote systems.

None of those arrangements requires a blockchain. A server can maintain account balances and game records in an ordinary database. A browser can display animation produced locally while showing information returned by that server. The visual experience alone reveals little about the underlying architecture.

This is also why an app download and browser access do not define opposing financial models. Either interface can connect to a conventional payment system, a crypto payment service, or a mixture of both. Distribution tells you how the product reaches the player. It does not identify the system that records ownership or enforces its rules.

DailyCoin’s analysis of DeFi front ends and smart contracts examines the separation between a website and the programs it accesses. The same distinction helps when assessing a game: its interface and the system executing its rules need to be identified separately.

Accepting cryptocurrency adds a payment method. A service might receive an asset directly or work through a payment processor that monitors transfers and updates the service’s account records. The asset received and the balance displayed to the customer need not be represented in the same way.

For example, a hypothetical platform could accept a token transfer and then record a corresponding account credit in its own database. Subsequent game actions could take place entirely within that platform’s existing infrastructure. The blockchain transfer and the account credit would be connected operationally, but they would remain separate records.

A transaction hash can help identify the transfer. It does not, by itself, reveal the logic used to calculate an unrelated game result. To understand the product, the next question is what happened after payment: was only a balance updated, or did a transaction call code that changed the game’s state?

Casino catalogs illustrate why these labels need to stay precise. Slots are identified by their reel or grid layouts, symbols, paylines, and feature rules. Classic slots, video slots, and progressive jackpot formats describe aspects of the game or prize structure. Those descriptions do not specify a blockchain network.

Consider how little a slot’s format tells us about its payment infrastructure. A payline defines which symbol positions form a combination, and a bonus rule defines what triggers an additional feature. Neither tells us how a deposit reaches the account or where the outcome calculation runs. Spin Casino’s description of online slots in Canada focuses on those game formats and mechanics. It belongs to the product-description layer of the analysis, separate from evidence about a wallet integration or a blockchain contract.

That separation prevents a familiar classification error: treating a digital casino game as an on-chain game simply because both are discussed alongside cryptocurrency. To establish a blockchain connection, identify the actual payment flow, asset record or executed game action. The slot label alone supplies none of those details.

The same discipline applies to a product described as a blockchain game. That label could refer to tokenized items while the match itself runs on a server. An ownership record and a record of the rules being executed are different kinds of evidence.

To understand on-chain gameplay, look for the programs that govern actions and store their consequences. Ethereum’s introduction to smart contracts describes contracts as code and state at an address on the blockchain. Transactions can call their functions, and execution follows the programmed rules.

In a hypothetical turn-based game, a contract could check whose turn it is, determine whether a move is permitted, and update the board. Recording only a collectible associated with that game would be a narrower use of the technology. The board and its rules might still be managed elsewhere.

Products can also combine these approaches. Some assets or actions may be recorded on-chain while other systems remain on servers. The interface can stay off-chain even when the underlying game logic runs in contracts. A claim of fully on-chain gameplay therefore needs a clear account of which rules and state are included, plus any outside data on which they depend.

When reading a product description, follow one action from start to finish. Identify what the player submits, which system processes it, and where the resulting change is recorded. That gives “online,” “crypto-enabled,” and “on-chain” concrete meanings that a logo, wallet connection, or token name cannot supply.

#5163. Mercado Bitcoin Said Its Hack Was Contained, But Blockchain Data Tells a Different Story

Mercado Bitcoin Said Its Hack Was Contained, But Blockchain Data Tells a Different Story

An attacker drained Mercado Bitcoin-linked deposit addresses nearly four hours after the Brazilian exchange said it had contained a security breach, new blockchain research shows.

Bitquery's analysis, updated Thursday, traces more than $48 million in stolen assets across 11 blockchains. Its findings challenge the exchange's claim that it stopped the attack quickly.

The Bitcoin exchange announced at 9:56 a.m. Brazil time on November 2 that it had quickly contained the incident. Bitquery says 36,042 Ethereum customer deposit addresses were emptied between 9:27 a.m. and 1:56 p.m. Brazil time.

Those addresses held roughly $266,000, a small fraction of the total theft. But the attacker could still move those funds after the exchange’s announcement.

A customer deposit address works much like a personal receiving account for cryptocurrency. The exchange later gathers those coins into a shared online wallet, called a hot wallet, to process everyday transactions. Moving funds from a deposit address requires its private key, the secret that authorizes transfers.

Bitquery says the withdrawals were authorized directly by the deposit addresses, suggesting the attacker had access to their private keys or to a system capable of signing transactions on their behalf.

“That needs a key for each address, or a way into the system that signs for them,” the researchers explained. They warned that exchanges typically generate deposit keys from a single master key, meaning the attacker may still be able to access other customer addresses.

The amount stolen is also disputed. Initial estimates put the amount above $40 million, while Mercado Bitcoin's updated FAQ now puts affected assets at about $36.3 million. Bitquery estimates that $48.6 million was stolen across 11 blockchains.

Mercado Bitcoin's public updates have not explained the gap between its containment claim and the later transfers. The company assured customers it would cover user losses with its own funds.

Bitquery warns customers against reusing old deposit addresses until the exchange confirms they are safe. Mercado Bitcoin's reopening plan begins November 9 with balance viewing only; deposits, withdrawals and trading have no restart date.

With price currently trading at $1.096, XRP has already recorded another substantial drop. The market positioning of the asset remains weak, as XRP is trading below its major moving averages. Higher lows and fundamental improvements are two main priorities for the asset right now.

XRP's last bullish hope was a short recovery rally towards the $1.34 price threshold. It failed to hold on to that momentum and tumbled towards the area where buyers previously stopped the summer decline. From approximately $1.34, XRP lost roughly 18% of its value and lost everything it built up throughout the recovery.

But where would XRP finally settle down? Realistically, the closest support is the $1.075 level, matching the latest session's low, followed by the $1.03–$1.05 range and the $0.99–$1.00 area, both psychological and technical. A breakdown below, unfortunately, would put the summer bottom under pressure and open the way to further weakness.

But even if XRP is oversold, with RSI below 30, bulls might still stay sidelined. The XRP Ledger activated the fixCleanup3_4_0 amendment on November 4. It removed an exploit that, under certain conditions, let accounts authorized to burn an issuer's tokens also mint them. The native supply of XRP has not been affected, luckily, but the amendment is not a factor that can help XRP reach key market levels.

In a case, where bulls somehow wake up, a recovery towards $1.15 and $1.20 is the main priority, while a proper trend reversal would require a move toward the moving averages around $1.30–$1.35.

Whether buyers can defend the $1 level or not is the main test for the asset right now. Without substantial volume, a short-lived price bounce here won't change the situation as a whole, unfortunately.

NEAR entered November under pressure after losing much of its September advance. After briefly reaching approximately $6 in October, the token fell toward $3.66 on November 9, according to the daily NEAR/USDT chart.

That represented a decline of roughly 39% from the local peak and put NEAR back at an important moving-average support zone.

Trading activity has also weakened alongside the price. Volume remains substantially below the levels seen during September’s breakout, suggesting that buyers have not yet returned with comparable strength.

However, lower volume does not necessarily confirm that selling pressure has disappeared. NEAR continues to form lower highs, while recovery attempts remain below its shorter-term moving averages.

Institutional exposure remains part of the investment case. Bitwise’s spot NEAR ETF, launched on September 29, held approximately 15.69 million NEAR worth $58.21 million as of Nov. 5. The fund reported that 99% of its holdings were staked.

Hyperliquid keeps going down and has recently violated an important moving average. It's now trading at $75, going further into downtrend, despite the strong fundamental background around Hyperliquid: Hyperliquid Strategies disclosure and a potential approval by the U.S. futures commission.

The broader market access, however, isn't something that the majority of retail investors consider a bullish catalyst, unfortunately. The asset has not yet found a strong bullish case. It's unlikely to be institutional too.

Technically, the bounce of HYPE/USDT could happen on 200 EMA, especially with a volume uptick and the recovery of the market in general. However, the selling pressure still overweights the buying support, according to exchange flows.

The netflow stays negative, and Hyperliquid is only yet to catch up with the bullish flow of the market. RSI confirms the thesis, moving around 40 and suggesting a bearish momentum, or a sideways movement at least. Volume should also surge substantially.

Key price levels for HYPE are: $72–$73 as the closest support level, $68 as the longer-term moving average, and $78–$80 as the first resistance level. Several moving averages sit at approximately $81–$85, so a breakthrough there should become a foundation for a price recovery.

Stellar already lost an important psychological level of $0.15, and there's a real scenario where XLM breaks down even more.

37% is the current recorded loss from its September peak of $0.235. The correction is rapidly erasing the recovery it has been building and finally invalidating it in October. The price is back in the accumulation range that was present back in May.

XLM moves below all major moving averages, with most of them aiming downwards and hinting at the aggravation of the current trend on the market.

With RSI and volume moving sideways or showing a descent, bear trend keeps the upper hand with sustained pressure on the price going further. The only positive signal could be the fact that RSI temporarily violated the reading of 30, which could be the sign of XLM approaching an oversold zone.

From a fundamental perspective, the Bell Protocol upgrade number 30 is the only thing that could set XLM apart from the rest of the market, with the vote scheduled for November 23.

The update will introduce: muxed contract addresses (ability to serve multiple users from a single smart contract), post-quantum signature verification and more.

In order to make the network more responsive, resilient and stronger in the future, millisecond ledger timing is also coming. It won't make the network faster on its own after the upgrade, but it opens up possibilities for developers to improve the network in the future.
